name: Kashmir
tagline: Lake houses, saffron karewas and shepherd meadows
meta_description: Plan Kashmir with locals' facts: houseboats on Dal, Gulmarg gondola, Pampore saffron, Gurez, real bus and Sumo fares, and honest budgets for 2026.
summary: Kashmir is a 135 km long valley at about 1,600 m, ringed by the Pir Panjal and the Great Himalaya. Come April to June for tulips and meadows, September to November for chinar and saffron, January to March for snow in Gulmarg. Six to eight nights covers Srinagar, Gulmarg, Pahalgam and Sonamarg.
intro: We call Kashmir the hive that was once a lake. The valley floor sits at roughly 1,600 m, flat as a tabletop, with the Jhelum winding through it and the Pir Panjal walling it to the south and west. Srinagar spreads around Dal Lake, where families still live and farm on the water. Around the rim, side valleys climb to meadows the Kashmiris call marg: Gulmarg, Sonamarg, Yusmarg. Each one is a day trip from the city, and each has its own season.

Most visitors rush the classic loop of Srinagar, Gulmarg and Pahalgam in five days. That works, but the valley rewards slower travel. Stay a night on a houseboat and you will hear the dawn vegetable market on the lake. Walk the Mughal gardens in October and the chinar leaves turn copper. Drive to Pampore in late October and the karewa plateaus are purple with saffron crocus. Cross the Razdan Pass to Gurez and you meet Shina-speaking villages in log houses below a pyramid peak named after a poet-queen.

Kashmir is also one of the easiest Himalayan regions to do on a budget. Shared Sumos link Srinagar with every valley for a few hundred rupees a seat, JKTDC runs government huts in Pahalgam, Sonamarg, Gulmarg, Yusmarg, Doodhpathri and Gurez, and houseboats on Dal and Nigeen offer simple rooms at guesthouse prices. Food is cheap and filling: noon chai and girda bread for breakfast, rajma and rice at roadside dhabas, a wazwan dinner when you want to splurge.

A practical note. Kashmir sees periodic security advisories, road closures and strikes, and some meadows have been closed to visitors at times. None of this is a reason to skip the valley, but plan with buffer days and check current advisories before you travel. Prepaid SIMs from outside Jammu and Kashmir generally do not work here; postpaid connections do. Carry photo ID everywhere, and expect police and army checkposts on roads to Gurez and other border areas.

story.title: The lake that became a valley

chapters.heading: Satisar, the drained lake
chapters.text: Kashmiri tradition, recorded in the Nilamata Purana, says the valley was once a great lake called Satisar, drained by the sage Kashyapa so people could settle. Geologists tell a parallel story. The flat-topped plateaus that rise above the valley floor, called karewas, are layers of old lake sediment laid down when the Jhelum basin was dammed. Those karewas matter to travellers today, because their well-drained soil is where Kashmir grows its saffron and almonds. Drive south from Srinagar to Pampore and you climb onto one. In late October the karewa at Pampore turns purple with crocus flowers, and families pick them at dawn before the petals open fully.

chapters.heading: Gardens built around water
chapters.text: The Mughal emperor Jahangir and his wife Nur Jahan moved their court to Kashmir for the summer at least 13 times. In 1619 Jahangir laid out Shalimar Bagh on the north-east shore of Dal Lake, fed by a central channel, the Shah Nahar, running down three terraces. In 1633 Nur Jahan's brother Asif Khan built Nishat Bagh nearby with twelve terraces. The engineering is the point: mountain springs and streams were led through stone channels, chutes and fountain basins purely by gravity. Shade came from chinar trees, the oriental plane, which tradition says reached Kashmir with Persian preachers in the 14th century. Today every chinar is registered as state property.

chapters.heading: Wood, wool and painted paper
chapters.text: Srinagar's old city is a working museum of craft. The Khanqah-e-Moula, first built in 1395 on the Jhelum bank to honour the Persian preacher Mir Sayyid Ali Hamadani, is a wooden shrine with papier-mache interiors. The Jamia Masjid at Nowhatta, begun in 1394, rests on 378 deodar columns. In the lanes around them, artisans still carve walnut wood, paint papier-mache boxes, embroider sozni shawls and weave carpets knot by knot. European demand for Kashmir shawls in the 19th century made the craft famous worldwide. In November 2021 UNESCO named Srinagar a Creative City for crafts and folk art, the second Indian city in that category after Jaipur.

chapters.heading: The herders' calendar
chapters.text: Long before tourists, the high meadows belonged to herders. Pahalgam means village of the shepherds in Kashmiri. Every spring Gujjar and Bakarwal families, listed as a Scheduled Tribe since 1991, drive goats, sheep and buffalo from the Jammu plains over the Pir Panjal and Banihal passes to summer pastures around Pahalgam, Sonamarg, Doodhpathri and Gurez, and walk back down before the snow. You will meet them on the road in May and October, and see their mud and timber huts in the meadows all summer. Gulmarg itself was renamed from Gaurimarg by Sultan Yousuf Shah Chak, husband of the poet Habba Khatoon, in the 16th century.

highlights.title: Sleep on Dal Lake
highlights.text: Houseboats exist because the Dogra rulers did not allow outsiders to own land, so British visitors built floating homes instead. Today budget boats on the inner Dal and Nigeen cost about the same as a guesthouse. Wake at 5 am and take a shikara to the floating vegetable market.

highlights.title: Walk the Mughal gardens
highlights.text: Shalimar (1619), Nishat (1633), Chashme Shahi and Pari Mahal line the Zabarwan foothills above Dal Lake. Go early on a weekday, follow the water channels uphill terrace by terrace, and come back in October when the chinar trees turn red and copper.

highlights.title: Ride to Apharwat
highlights.text: The Gulmarg Gondola climbs in two phases from the meadow at 2,650 m to Kongdori and then close to 4,000 m on Apharwat. Book slots online, go early before cloud builds, and carry a warm layer even in June. In winter the upper bowls are a serious ski terrain.

highlights.title: Follow the Lidder upstream
highlights.text: From Pahalgam the East and West Lidder rivers lead to Chandanwari, Betaab Valley and Aru. Aru, 12 km up, is the start of treks to the Kolahoi Glacier and the Tarsar and Marsar lakes. Local union taxis run the valley circuits at fixed rates.

highlights.title: Saffron on the karewas
highlights.text: Kashmir saffron, grown mainly on the Pampore karewas 15 km from Srinagar, received a Geographical Indication tag in May 2020. Visit from late October to mid November to see the crocus flowers picked at dawn, then buy directly from growers or the trading centre at Dussu.

highlights.title: Cross into Gurez
highlights.text: A 123 km road from Srinagar climbs over the Razdan Pass to the Kishanganga valley, where Shina-speaking villages of log houses sit below the pyramid-shaped Habba Khatoon peak. The pass is snowbound for about half the year, so go between June and October.

money_savers: Use shared Sumos from Srinagar's taxi stands to Tangmarg, Pahalgam and Sonamarg for a few hundred rupees a seat instead of a full-day cab.
Book JKTDC huts and hotels directly on jktdc.co.in, where government rates in Pahalgam, Sonamarg, Yusmarg and Gurez undercut private resorts.
Negotiate houseboat rooms on Nigeen or the inner Dal in person in October, November and March, when rates often fall by a third or more.
Buy Gulmarg Gondola tickets online for the time slot you want; touts at the base charge extra for the same ticket.
Eat breakfast the Kashmiri way with nun chai and girda or lavasa bread from a neighbourhood kandur bakery for under ₹100.
Take the Katra–Srinagar Vande Bharat train (about 3 hours, chair car about ₹700–800) instead of a 9-hour taxi from Jammu.
getting_there: Most travellers fly into Srinagar airport, about 12 km from the city centre, with non-stop flights from Delhi (about 1 h 30 min), Mumbai, Bengaluru, Kolkata and other cities. Since June 2025 the Udhampur–Srinagar–Baramulla rail link has carried Vande Bharat trains from Shri Mata Vaishno Devi Katra to Srinagar in about 3 hours, crossing the Chenab rail bridge; chair car fares were about ₹715 at launch. Local DEMU trains run along the valley between Banihal and Baramulla, stopping at Anantnag, Pampore and Srinagar. By road, NH44 from Jammu is about 250 km and 7–9 hours through the Banihal tunnels, with shared Sumos and JKSRTC buses from Jammu. The Mughal Road via Peer Ki Gali links Poonch to Shopian in summer. Check current status before you travel; landslides and snow can close roads for days.
permits: Indian citizens need no permit for Srinagar, Gulmarg, Pahalgam, Sonamarg, Doodhpathri or Yusmarg. For Gurez, Indians register with photo ID (Aadhaar is easiest) at army and police checkposts along the road; foreign nationals have needed prior permission from the Deputy Commissioner in Bandipora. The Amarnath Yatra requires advance registration with the Shri Amarnathji Shrine Board and a compulsory health certificate. Dachigam National Park needs a permit from the Wildlife Department in Srinagar. Rules change; check current status before you travel.

months.summary: January sits inside Chillai Kalan, the 40 coldest days of the Kashmiri winter that run from 21 December to the end of January. Dal Lake can freeze at the edges, and Srinagar wakes to fog and smoke from kangris. Gulmarg has deep snow and the ski season is in full swing. Roads to Gulmarg are kept open; Sonamarg is now reachable through the Z-Morh tunnel. Pack thermal layers and expect short power cuts.
months.tip: Book Gulmarg rooms for the first fortnight of January early, because the New Year crowd stays on.

months.summary: February is the best month for snow sports in Gulmarg, with a deep base and clearer days than January. Skiers come from across India and abroad, and the gondola's upper phase opens to the Apharwat bowls when avalanche conditions allow. Srinagar stays cold and quiet, and houseboat owners offer winter discounts. Pahalgam is under snow and good for a sledge-and-snow day trip from the city.
months.tip: Hire ski gear in Gulmarg rather than carrying it; rental shops near the gondola base cover most sizes.

months.weather: Srinagar 3 to 14 °C, rain and late snow
months.summary: March is the turn of the season. Almond trees blossom in Srinagar's Badamwari garden below Hari Parbat, snow lingers in Gulmarg, and the tulip garden usually opens at the end of the month. Days can swing between sun and cold rain, so pack a waterproof. Hotel prices are still low until the tulip rush begins, which makes the first three weeks good value.
months.tip: Watch the tulip garden's official opening announcement before fixing dates; bloom depends on the weather.

months.summary: April is tulip month. The Indira Gandhi Memorial Tulip Garden at the foot of the Zabarwan range is in bloom for three to four weeks, and the Mughal gardens fill with spring flowers. Snow is retreating from Pahalgam and Gulmarg, the meadows are turning green, and the Lidder runs high and clear. This is peak domestic season, so book houseboats and flights early.
months.tip: Visit the tulip garden at opening time on a weekday to avoid the 11 am to 3 pm crowd.

months.summary: May is warm in Srinagar and fresh in the hills. Sonamarg's road and the Thajiwas glacier walk open, Doodhpathri and Yusmarg meadows are green, and the Gujjar and Bakarwal herders are moving up with their flocks. School holidays in north India begin late in the month, so prices climb. The Kheer Bhawani mela at Tulmulla sometimes falls in late May.
months.tip: Plan the meadows on weekdays; Srinagar families fill Doodhpathri and Yusmarg on Sundays.

months.summary: June is the busiest month. Every hotel in Pahalgam, Gulmarg and Sonamarg is in demand, and Srinagar can feel hot by afternoon. It is also when the high country opens: the Razdan Pass road to Gurez is usually clear, Aru's trails lead to Lidderwat and beyond, and wildflowers fill the margs. The Kheer Bhawani mela usually falls this month.
months.tip: Pre-book everything in June, including the gondola, because walk-in rates and availability are poor.

months.summary: July brings the Amarnath Yatra, when tens of thousands of pilgrims move through Pahalgam and Baltal near Sonamarg. Roads carry convoys, and some days have traffic restrictions. Away from the yatra routes the season is good: Kashmir gets far less monsoon rain than the outer Himalaya, and the Great Lakes and Tarsar Marsar treks are open. Gurez and Yusmarg are calm and green.
months.tip: If you are not a pilgrim, avoid driving the Pahalgam or Sonamarg roads on yatra convoy mornings.

months.summary: August continues the yatra until Raksha Bandhan, after which Pahalgam and Sonamarg quieten. This is prime trekking time for the high lakes, and the herders' camps are full in the meadows. Afternoon showers and occasional landslides affect roads, especially on the Jammu highway, so leave a buffer day before your flight.
months.tip: Carry a light rain shell for afternoon showers on the meadows.

months.summary: September is one of our favourite months. Skies clear, crowds drop after the yatra, hotel rates soften, and apple orchards around Sopore and Shopian are being harvested. Gurez is golden and the Razdan Pass is still open. Treks remain open until about mid-month in the high lakes. Nights start to bite above 2,500 m.
months.tip: Combine Gurez with Sonamarg this month; both are at their clearest.

months.summary: October is chinar and saffron month. The plane trees in Naseem Bagh, Nishat and along the Boulevard turn yellow, then red, and from the last week the Pampore karewas bloom purple with crocus. Herders bring their flocks down, and hangul stags call in Dachigam during the rut. Days are sunny, nights near freezing, and prices fall after the Durga Puja and Diwali rush.
months.tip: Plan Pampore for the final week of October or first week of November and go at dawn.

months.weather: Srinagar −1 to 15 °C, dry, first snow on peaks
months.summary: November is quiet and cheap. The saffron harvest runs into the first half of the month, the last chinar leaves fall, and the first snow dusts Gulmarg and the Pir Panjal. Mornings are foggy in Srinagar. Houseboats and hotels offer their lowest rates of the year, and the city feels local again.
months.tip: Ask your houseboat for a kangri or a heater before you check in; nights drop below zero.

months.summary: December begins grey and cold, and Chillai Kalan starts on 21 December. Gulmarg usually has skiable snow by Christmas, when it fills with New Year visitors. Harissa, a slow-cooked mutton and rice dish, appears in Srinagar's old city shops on winter mornings. Flights can be delayed by fog, so keep a day spare.
months.tip: Try harissa at dawn in Srinagar's old city; shops sell out by mid-morning.

faqs.q: Is Kashmir safe for tourists right now?
faqs.a: Millions of domestic tourists visit Kashmir each year and the main circuits of Srinagar, Gulmarg, Pahalgam and Sonamarg are heavily used. Security situations can change quickly, though, and some meadows and roads have been closed to visitors at times. Check current advisories before you travel, register with your hotel, carry photo ID, follow local police instructions, and keep a buffer day in case of strikes or road closures.

faqs.q: What is the best time to visit Kashmir?
faqs.a: April to June for tulips, green meadows and open roads; September to November for clear skies, chinar colours and the saffron harvest; January to March for snow and skiing in Gulmarg. July and August are fine for treks and Gurez but busy on the Amarnath Yatra routes through Pahalgam and Sonamarg. December and January are very cold but beautiful.

faqs.q: How many days do I need for Kashmir?
faqs.a: Six to eight nights is ideal: three in Srinagar including a houseboat night, one or two in Gulmarg, and two or three in Pahalgam, with a Sonamarg day trip. Five nights is the minimum for the classic loop. Add three nights for Gurez, and four to seven for a trek such as Tarsar Marsar or the Great Lakes.

faqs.q: How much does a Kashmir trip cost per person?
faqs.a: On a saver budget with houseboat rooms, JKTDC huts and shared Sumos, plan ₹2,500–4,000 a day per person, so about ₹15,000–25,000 for six nights excluding travel to Srinagar. A comfort trip with a private car and good hotels runs ₹7,000–12,000 a day. Top hotels such as the Khyber and LaLiT push it to ₹20,000–45,000 a day.

faqs.q: Will my mobile SIM work in Kashmir?
faqs.a: Postpaid connections from any Indian operator work in Jammu and Kashmir. Prepaid SIMs issued outside J&K generally do not work, under a long-standing security rule. Buy a local prepaid SIM in Srinagar with your ID and a local reference, or use hotel Wi-Fi. Coverage is good in Srinagar and the main resorts, patchy in Gurez, and absent on high treks. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit to visit Kashmir?
faqs.a: Indian citizens need no permit for the main valley. Gurez needs registration at checkposts with photo ID, and foreigners have needed prior permission from the Bandipora administration. Amarnath pilgrims must register with the Shrine Board and carry a health certificate. Dachigam needs a Wildlife Department permit. Foreign nationals should carry passports at all times. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: When does it snow in Kashmir?
faqs.a: Gulmarg usually gets reliable snow from mid-December to March, and the upper gondola slopes can hold snow into April. Srinagar sees a few snowfalls between late December and February. Pahalgam and Sonamarg are under snow from December to March. If you want guaranteed snow underfoot for a family trip, February in Gulmarg is the safest bet.

faqs.q: Should we stay on a houseboat or in a hotel?
faqs.a: Do both. One or two nights on a houseboat is a Srinagar experience you cannot get elsewhere: carved walnut interiors, a shikara at the door and the dawn market. Budget boats on Nigeen and the inner Dal cost ₹1,500–3,000 a room, deluxe boats far more. Hotels on the Boulevard or Rajbagh are easier for families with heavy luggage or limited mobility.

faqs.q: Can I reach Kashmir by train?
faqs.a: Yes. Since June 2025 Vande Bharat trains run from Shri Mata Vaishno Devi Katra to Srinagar in about 3 hours, and local trains link Banihal, Anantnag, Pampore, Srinagar and Baramulla. Reach Katra by train from Delhi and other cities, then change. Book early in season, and check current timetables and through-train plans before you travel.
